title: Pro-Habsburg Spain
capsule: Following the death of Charles II of Spain in November 1700 without an heir, the War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714) divided the Iberian Peninsula between Bourbon supporters (principally Castile) and those who backed the Austrian Habsburg claimant Archduke Charles (III). From roughly 1705–1710 the archduke, recognized as Charles III by the Grand Alliance, controlled Catalonia, Aragon, Valencia, and much of eastern Spain, with Barcelona as his capital. The allied cause collapsed after the Holy Roman Emperor Joseph I died in 1711 and the archduke became Emperor Charles VI, removing the diplomatic rationale for a united Habsburg Spain; the Treaty of Utrecht (1713) confirmed Philip V's Bourbon monarchy over the whole peninsula.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The territorial extent of pro-Habsburg control in Spain during 1702–1709 is well documented through military campaign records and diplomatic correspondence, though front lines shifted seasonally.
